title: pool-heartbeat-spelunking-log
content:
Notes-to-self: weird heartbeat/eviction pattern observed in dedicated pool 'd-pool-west-2a' during last 72h. This is a running scratchpad — choppy bullets, commands I ran, raw snippets, and immediate hypotheses.

Summary of incident (short)
- Symptoms: sudden capacity thrash (node count oscillates), long tail of warmup latency spikes, repeated pod re-scheduling that coincides with autoscaler decisions. Apps saw 503s intermittently and request latency jumps.
- Window: 2026-03-07 03:40 -> 2026-03-09 14:00 (UTC)
- Affected: dedicated GPU pool d-pool-west-2a, serving-runtime qps-heavy routes (text-gen, chat).

What I saw (timeline + raw breadcrumbs)
2026-03-07T03:42Z - Alert from PagerDuty: "d-pool-west-2a node down -> fallback to shared-hosted".
2026-03-07T03:45Z - Datadog event: autoscaler scaled down nodes from 18 -> 6 in ~3m.
2026-03-07T03:47Z - Running top-level check: (kubectl output snippet)
$ kubectl get pods -n redwood-serving -o wide --selector=pool=d-pool-west-2a
NAME                                    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   NODE
inference-0                             1/1     Running   0          2d    ip-10-0-3-12
inference-1                             1/1     Running   0          2d    ip-10-0-3-15
inference-burst-7                       0/1     Pending   0          5m    <none>

2026-03-07T03:48Z - Describe pending pod:
$ kubectl describe pod inference-burst-7 -n redwood-serving
Events:
  Type     Reason            Age   From                Message
  ----     ------            ----  ----                -------
  Warning  FailedScheduling  2m    default-scheduler   0/20 nodes are available: 12 Insufficient gpu, 8 node(s) had taint {dedicated: gpu}, that the pod didn't tolerate.

Raw autoscaler log (tail):
[03:44:30] scale-controller: decision=scale-down target=6 reason=idle-threshold
[03:44:33] scale-controller: launching drain on node ip-10-0-3-18
[03:44:38] kubelet: Evicting pods due to node maintenance: pod=inference-3
[03:46:10] scale-controller: decision=scale-up target=18 reason=queued-demand
[03:46:12] scale-controller: starting provisioning of 12 nodes (spot mix)
[03:47:45] infra: provisioning failed for 4 instances: error=InsufficientCapacity
[03:48:10] scale-controller: scaled to 14 live nodes

Notes: provisioning failures correlate with the longest warmup gaps. Many of the new nodes came up with GPU drivers not ready for ~2-3 mins which caused pods to stay Pending.

Commands I ran while investigating (and outputs)
- Check GPU device readiness on node (run ssh to node)
$ ssh infra-admin@ip-10-0-3-20 'nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,driver_version,temperature.gpu --format=csv'
name, driver_version, temperature.gpu
A100-SXM4-40GB, 535.104.05, 43 C

- Kube events for a node that flapped:
$ kubectl get events --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' -n redwood-serving | tail -n 40
2026-03-07T03:44:33Z  Normal  ScaleDown  scale-controller  node/ip-10-0-3-18 scheduled for scale-down
2026-03-07T03:44:38Z  Warning Eviction    kubelet           Pod inference-3 evicted: node pressure
2026-03-07T03:46:12Z  Normal  Provisioning  infra-service     launching spot instances (mix: p4d,p3)
2026-03-07T03:47:45Z  Error   ProvisionFail infra-service     InsufficientCapacity for p4d in us-west-2a

Observed metrics (rough)
- avg token latency rose 2.1x for heavy routes when live nodes dropped below 12.
- kube-scheduler scheduling_attempts_per_min spiked from 15 -> 180.
- GPU utilization on remaining nodes peaked at 94% for ~9m before new nodes registered.

Hypotheses (brain dump)
1) Autoscaler configured with aggressive scale-down window (idle-after 5m) causing cascade when workload has microbursts. Scale-down decided, nodes drained, queued pods blocked waiting for new nodes, autoscaler reacts late and scales up -> provisioning failures (spot insufficiency) produce partial recovery -> repeat.
2) Provisioning mix includes spot types that are often InsufficientCapacity in the AZ; fallback to other shapes is slow. Should prefer guaranteed shapes for reserved pools.
3) Node bootstrap (GPU driver or nvidia-container-runtime) sometimes takes longer than instance ready signal used by autoscaler leading to pods in Pending state despite nodes being 'Ready'. Missed readiness probe timing.
4) Taints/tolerations mismatch: some pool-level taints are not matched by ephemeral worker pods causing them to remain unschedulable.
5) Kube scheduler is thrashing because we have multiple anti-affinity/zone constraints combined with pack-scheduling heuristics; scale-down chooses nodes that contain many packed pods causing re-schedules across nodes.

Short experiments I ran + results
- Temporarily increased scale-down window from 5m -> 15m on staging pool (command: kubectl -n kube-system edit configmap autoscaler-config) -> observed no oscillation for 1h during controlled burst test. Good sign (supports hyp 1).
- Forced allocation to non-spot shapes for a small test: set preferred instanceTypes to [c6i,g5] -> provisioning steady, warmups reduced by ~40s on average.
- Added nodeBootProbe check in kubelet systemd unit to ensure nvidia modules loaded before marking Ready -> reduced Pending-to-Ready delta from 150s -> 40s in a small canary.

Error snippets captured
- "0/20 nodes are available: 12 Insufficient gpu" (scheduler)
- "InsufficientCapacity: Could not fulfill requested capacity" (cloud infra)
- kubelet log: "container runtime failed to start container: failed to setup nvidia runtime: device not found"

Immediate mitigations (short-term playbook)
- Increase scale-down cooldown to 10m for dedicated pools serving bursty routes.
- Switch preferred provisioning to include a small percentage of on-demand/gpu-guaranteed nodes to avoid full-spot exhaustion in high-burst windows. (temp change via infra-service)
- Add a small buffer (minNodes) to pool to keep baseline capacity >= 12 for heavy routes.
- Add post-provision check: only mark node as schedulable after nvidia-smi returns GPUs and driver version > 535.x. Implemented as init script in AMI.

Longer-term bets / design changes to consider
- Autoscaler policies that are demand-shape-aware: use request waveform (qps short-term) to compute minimum hold time to avoid scaling down through microbursts.
- Prefer warm standby nodes (cheap-sized instances kept warm with no serving processes until needed). Might reduce cold-start cost vs spot churn.
- Improve instance selection: prefer shapes with historical provisioning success rate in AZ. Feed back provisioning success metrics into autoscaler decisions.
- Make the scheduler GPU-aware beyond counting: consider per-GPU-memory fragmentation when placing shards.

Next steps (practical TODOs)
- [ ] Push autoscaler scale-down window change to prod for the affected pool (owner: Jia). JIRA INF-4721 updated.
- [ ] Add nvidia driver readiness gating to AMI (owner: Leo). quick test in canary first.
- [ ] Create a Datadog dashboard that shows provisioning-failures by instance-type and AZ (owner: me).
- [ ] Run 2h synthetic microburst test after changes to validate no oscillation.

Random heuristics / things to watch
- If scheduling_attempts_per_min > 120 and avg token latency > baseline*1.5 -> likely autoscaler thrash.
- Provisioning fail rate > 7% over 30m window -> switch to fallback on-demand pool for that time window.

Questions I still have / to confirm
- Are there any downstream rate-limits (cloud account-level) that could exacerbate provisioning delays? (ask infra team)
- Is the spot instance pool configured to fall back to other instance types quickly enough? What are the actual fallbacks?
- Confirm whether drain strategy is 'evict immediately' or 'graceful with disruption budget' for these nodes.

End of notes. This is intentionally informal; will refine into a playbook if mitigations prove effective in the next 72h.

Quicklog: recent command refs
- kubectl get pods -n redwood-serving --selector=pool=d-pool-west-2a -o wide
- kubectl describe pod <pod> -n redwood-serving
- kubectl get events -n redwood-serving --sort-by='.lastTimestamp'
- ssh infra-admin@<node> 'nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,driver_version --format=csv'
